Surah Ta-Ha

Surah Ta-Ha is Meccan and has one hundred and thirty-five verses, according to the Kufan count.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Ta-Ha﴾. He emphasized (fakhkhama) the ṭāʾ (ṭāʾ mufakhkhama, the heavy/emphatic pronunciation) because of its elevated quality (istiʿlāʾ). Abu ʿAmr inclined the hāʾ (imālah, a fronting of the vowel toward i), while Ḥamzah, ʿAlī, Khalaf and Abu Bakr inclined both letters; the others emphasized both, in accordance with the original form. As for what has been related from Mujahid, al-Hasan, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, ʿAṭāʾ and others, that its meaning is "O man," if it is authentically established then it is apparent; otherwise, the truth is what is mentioned in Surah al-Baqarah.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 2:

﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you﴾ If Ta-Ha is taken as an enumeration of the names of the letters, then it is the beginning of a statement. If you take it as the name of the sura, it may be a predicate referring to it, and it is then in the position of the subject (mubtada'). The word "al-Qur'an" is an explicit noun placed in the position of a pronoun, because they are [the sura is] "Qur'an." It may also be an answer to it (the oath), and it is an oath (qasam): ﴿that you should be distressed﴾, that you should be exhausted, because of your excessive grief over them and over their disbelief, and your anguish that they should not believe; or [it refers] to standing in prayer at night. It is narrated that: "He (ﷺ) prayed at night until his feet swelled, and Jibril said to him: 'Spare yourself, for your self has a right over you.'" That is: We did not send it down so that you would wear out yourself with worship, and you were not sent except with the easy, upright religion (al-hanifiyya al-samha).

﴿Except as a reminder﴾ is a discontinuous exception (istithna' munqati', an exception whose excluded item is not of the same kind as what precedes it), meaning: "but We sent it down as a reminder." Or it is a circumstantial accusative (hal, a clause describing the state of the subject). ﴿For those who fear﴾: for those who fear God, or for those whose affair leads to fear (khashya, awe-filled fear of God). (p-357)

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on Surah 20, verse 4:**

﴿تَنْـزِيلا﴾ is a substitute (badal, a grammatical substitution of one noun for another) for "تَذْكِرَةً" if the latter is taken as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl, a noun in the accusative describing the state of the subject at the time of the action). It may also be in the accusative by an implied verb, "نَزَّلَ" (he sent down), or as an object of praise (al-madḥ), or "يَخْشى" may be its object (mafʿūl bih). The meaning is: Allah sent it down as a reminder for whoever fears, a revelation from Allah. ﴿مِمَّنْ خَلَقَ الأرْضَ والسَماواتِ﴾ is connected to "تَنْزِيلًا" as its complement (ṣila, the phrase that completes a noun's meaning). "العَلِي" is the plural of "العَلْياءِ," the feminine of "الأعْلى" (the highest). Describing the heavens as "العُلى" (the high ones) is clear evidence of the greatness of the power of their Creator.

﴿الرَحْمَنُ﴾ is in the nominative (*rafʿ*, the case of the subject) by way of praise (*ʿala al-madḥ*, "as an expression of praise"), meaning: He is ﴿the Most Merciful﴾. ﴿عَلى العَرْشِ﴾ ("on the Throne") is the predicate (*khabar*) of an omitted subject (*mubtadaʾ maḥdhūf*). ﴿اسْتَوى﴾ ("established") means *istawlā*, "took dominion," according to al-Zajjaj (Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, the grammarian).

He drew attention by mentioning the Throne, which is the greatest of created things, over anything else. It has also been said: since sitting upon the Throne, which is the king's couch, is something that accompanies kingship, they used it as a metaphor (*kināya*, a figurative expression) for dominion. So they say "so-and-so istawā upon the throne," meaning he ruled, even if he never actually sat on the couch at all. This is like your saying "so-and-so's hand is outstretched," meaning he is generous, even though he has no hand whatsoever.

The accepted position (*al-madhhab*) is the statement of ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him: "Istiwāʾ is not unknown; its modality (*takyīf*) is not conceivable; belief in it is obligatory; and asking about it is an innovation (*bidʿa*, a matter introduced into religion without basis)." This is because He, exalted is He, existed when there was no place, so He is as He was before creating place, unchanged from what He was.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 6:

﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ — "to Him belongs" is the predicate (khabar), and "whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth" is the subject (mubtada'), with the conjoined element (ma'tuf) following. ﴿And whatever is between them﴾ — that is, all of that is His dominion. ﴿And whatever is beneath the soil (al-thara)﴾ — that is, whatever is beneath the seven earths; or it is the rock that lies beneath the seventh earth.

﴿And if you speak aloud﴾, i.e., you raise your voice, ﴿then indeed He knows the secret﴾ that which you confide to another, ﴿and what is yet more hidden﴾ than that, which is what you let occur to your mind, or what you keep secret within yourself, and what you will keep secret within it in the future.

﴿Allah, there is no god but Him. To Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾ Meaning: He is one in His essence, even though the expressions of His attributes differ. This refutes their saying, "You invoke gods," when they heard His names, exalted is He. Al-husna is the feminine form of al-ahsan (the most beautiful).

**Verse 9: "And has there reached you the story of Musa?"**

﴿وَهَلْ﴾ (wa-hal), meaning: and indeed (وقد) ﴿أتاكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسى﴾ (atāka ḥadīthu Mūsā), meaning: its report has reached you. He follows it with the story of Musa, peace be upon him, so that (the Prophet) may take him as a model in bearing the burdens of prophethood with patience in the face of hardships, and so that he may attain the high rank just as Musa attained it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 20, verse 10:

﴿When he saw﴾ is an adverbial complement of time (*ẓarf*) governing an implied verb, meaning: at the time when he saw ﴿a fire﴾, such-and-such happened. Alternatively, it is a direct object of ﴿Remember﴾. It is related that Musa (peace be upon him) asked Shu'ayb for permission to go out to his mother, and he left with his family. A son was born to him on the road, on a dark, snowy night. He had lost the way, his livestock had scattered, and he had no water. He struck his flint, but it did not produce a spark. At that moment he saw a fire, as he supposed, but it was a light. ﴿So he said to his family: Wait here﴾, that is, stay in your place. ﴿Indeed I have perceived a fire﴾, that is, I have seen it. The verb *ās* (to perceive something reassuring) means seeing something that brings comfort. ﴿Perhaps I will bring you from it﴾: he framed the matter in terms of hope, so that he would not promise what he could not be certain of fulfilling. ﴿A brand﴾, a fire kindled in the tip of a stick or a wick. ﴿Or I may find at the fire guidance﴾, meaning people with guidance, or people who would show me the way. The sense of elevation (*isti'la'*) in ﴿at the fire﴾ is that the people of the fire occupy the place close to it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 11:

﴿When he came to it⦆ — that is, to the fire, he found a white fire blazing in a green tree from its base to its top. It was a tree of ʿunnab (jujube) or ʿawsaj (boxthorn), and he found no one near it. It is also narrated that whenever he sought to approach it, it moved away from him, and when he left it, it came close to him. Then ﴿he was called﴾, ﴿O Musa!﴾

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 12:

﴿Innī﴾ with a kasra on the hamza (inni), meaning: he was called, and it was said, "O Musa, indeed I [am]..." or because the calling (al-nida') is a form of speech, so it is treated as speech. With a fatha (anna), it is read by Makki and Abu 'Amr, meaning: he was called with "that I am [anā rabbuka]..." The pronoun is either the subject of the sentence (mubtada'), or an emphasis (ta'kid), or a separator (fasl). The pronoun is repeated to confirm knowledge and remove doubt. It is narrated that when he was called, "O Musa," he said, "Who is speaking?" (p-359) Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said, "I am your Lord [anā rabbuka]." So he knew that it was the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, because he heard it from all six directions and heard it with all of his limbs. ﴿So take off your sandals﴾ remove them, so that your feet may receive the blessing of the sacred valley. Or because they were made of the skin of a dead donkey that had not been tanned. Or because going barefoot is a display of humility before Allah, and for this reason the early generations (al-salaf) performed the circumambulation of the Ka'ba barefoot. The Qur'an indicates that this was a sign of respect for the place and its glorification. So he took them off and threw them behind the valley. ﴿Indeed you are in the sacred valley﴾ the purified or blessed one ﴿Tuwa﴾. Where it is read with tanwin (Tuwan) by al-Shami and al-Kufi, it is a proper noun for the valley and is a substitute (badal) for it. The others read it without tanwin, interpreting it as a place (al-buqʻa). Abu Zayd read it with a kasra on the ta' without tanwin.

﴿And I have chosen you﴾: I have selected you for prophethood (*nubuwwah*). Hamza reads "وَإنّا اخْتَرْناكَ" (*wa-innā ikhtarnāka*, "and indeed We have chosen you"). ﴿So listen to what is revealed﴾ to you. "To what is revealed" means either "to the one who is revealed," or "to the revelation." The *lam* in "لِما" (*li-mā*) is connected to "اسْتَمِعْ" (*istami'*, "listen"), while Abu connects it to "اخْتَرْتُكَ" (*ikhtartuka*, "I have chosen you").

Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me. ﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾

"Affirm My oneness (tawhid) and obey Me." ﴿And establish prayer for My remembrance﴾ so that you remember Me in it, because prayer includes remembrances (adhkar); or because I mentioned it in the scriptures and commanded it; or so that I mention you with praise and commendation; or for My remembrance specifically, unmixed with the remembrance of anyone else; or so that you remember Me without forgetting; or for the times of My remembrance, which are the prescribed times of prayer, based on His saying ﴿Indeed, prayer has been enjoined upon the believers as a decree of specified times﴾ [an-Nisa: 103]. Some have understood it as the remembrance of prayer after forgetting it, and this is valid if the governed noun (mudaf) is omitted, i.e., "for the remembrance of My prayer." This indicates that there is no obligation after tawhid greater than it.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 15:

﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾ without doubt. ﴿I almost conceal it﴾: "I want to" — according to al-Akhfash. It is also said that "almost" (akad) is here a particle of connection (silah). ﴿That I may reveal it﴾. It is said that this is one of the words with opposite meanings (al-adad), i.e., "I reveal it" or "I conceal it from the servants." So I do not say it is coming, because I intend to conceal it. Were it not for what has come in the reports about its coming, while its time is kept hidden, there would be wisdom in it, namely that if they do not know when it will rise, they would be in constant apprehension of it at every moment, because of what I have informed them of. ﴿So that every soul may be recompensed﴾ — this is connected to "coming" — ﴿for what it strives for﴾, by its striving, whether good or evil.

Surah 20, verse 16:

﴿So let not one who does not believe in it and follows his desire turn you away from it, lest you perish.﴾

Al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil): "Fa-la yasuddannaka 'anha" means: let them not divert you from working for the Hour, or from establishing the prayer, or from belief in the Resurrection. The address is to Musa, and what is meant by it is his community (ummah). "Man la yu'minu biha" means: one who does not affirm it. "Wa-ittaba'a hawahu" means: in opposing His command. "Fa-tardá" means: so that you perish.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾

[Translation of the grammatical analysis:]

"Mā" (what) is the subject (mubtada'), and "tilka" (that) is its predicate (khabar); "hiya" here carries the meaning of "hadhihi" (this). "Biyaminika" (in your right hand) is a circumstantial phrase (hal), and the sense of pointing (ishara) governs it: that is, "standing" in your right hand or "taken" in your right hand. Alternatively, "tilka" is a relative pronoun (mawsul) whose relative clause (silah) is "biyaminika" (in your right hand).

The question is asked for alerting (li-l-tanbih), so that the miracle that will occur through it happens after he has become certain of it; or for settling (li-l-tawtin), lest its transformation into a serpent should terrify him; or for putting him at ease (li-l-ina's) and removing awe (raf' al-haybah), so that he may converse.

﴿He said, "It is my staff; I lean on it"﴾ (أعْتَمِدُ عَلَيْها): I rely on it when I am weary, or when I stand at the head of the flock and at the place of leaping (al-ṭafra). ﴿And I beat down (leaves) with it for my flock﴾: I strike the leaves of trees with it for my sheep so that they may eat. ﴿And I have in it﴾: Ḥafṣ. ﴿Other uses (maʾārib)﴾: مَآرِبُ is the plural of مَأْرَبَةٌ, which may be vocalized in three ways, and it means need (al-ḥāja). ﴿Other﴾: أُخْرى. By analogy it should be أُخَرُ, but he said أُخْرى either to return it to the group (الجماعة) or for the sake of the rhyme of the verses (لِنَسَقِ الآيِ). The same applies to الكُبْرى. When he mentioned some of them, out of gratitude, he summarized the rest out of modesty about lengthy description, or so that he might ask the King, the All-Knowing, about them, and He would increase him in honor. As for the other uses (المَآرِبُ الأُخَرُ): it was that the staff would accompany him and converse with him, fight the enemy and the beasts of prey, become a rope that lengthens with the depth of the well, its two prongs becoming a bucket, and both becoming two candles at night. It carried his provisions, and he would plant it, and it would bear fruit of whatever he desired; and when he planted it, water would gush forth, and when he lifted it, the water would recede. It also protected him from venomous creatures (الهَوامّ). The addition beyond the answer serves to enumerate the blessings as an expression of gratitude, or because it is the answer to another question: when he said "It is my staff," he was asked, "What do you do with it?", so he began enumerating its benefits. (p-٣٦١)

"He said: 'Throw it down, O Musa.'" Cast down your staff, so that you may be startled by what you lean upon, and so that you will find rest only in Us, and see in it the full extent of the benefits it holds, so that you will rely upon Us in your needs.

﴿So he cast it down﴾ — he threw it. ﴿And behold, it was a serpent moving swiftly﴾ — walking quickly. It was said: it turned into a thu'ban (a large serpent) that swallowed up the rock and the tree; so when he saw it swallowing everything, he became afraid. The description "serpent" (ḥayya) is used here, and "thu'ban," which is the large kind of serpents, and "jann," which is the small kind in other places, because ḥayya (serpent) is a collective noun (ism jins) that applies to the male and the female, the young and the old. It was possible for it to turn into a yellow, slender serpent and then its body would grow until it became a thu'ban; so "jann" is meant for its initial state and "thu'ban" for its final state. Or, it was because it had the size of a thu'ban and the speed of a jann. It was also said that the distance between its two jaws was forty cubits.

"Allah said: ﴿Take it and fear not. We will return it to its former state.﴾

21 – When ﴿He said﴾ to him, His Lord, ﴿Take it and fear not,﴾ (Moses) was so free of fear that he put his hand into its mouth and seized it by its jaws. ﴿We will return it﴾ means We will restore it, ﴿to its former state.﴾ "Former" is the feminine form of "first" (al-awwal). The sirah (state, condition) is the condition in which a person is, whether natural or acquired. Originally it is a form (fi'lah) derived from al-sayr (going), like the rikbah (manner of riding) from al-rukub (riding). It was then used to mean condition and manner, and it is put in the accusative as an adverb of time/circumstance (zarf): i.e., "We will return it in its first manner," meaning in the state in which it was a staff. The meaning is: We will return it to being a staff as it was. This was shown to Moses during the address so that he would not be frightened of it when it turned into a serpent before Pharaoh."

Then He drew his attention to another sign, saying: ﴿And draw your hand to your side﴾, to your flank, under the armpit. The two sides (janahan) of a human being are his two flanks, and the original, borrowed meaning of "janahan" is the two wings of a bird; they were called "janahayn" because it inclines (yujnihuhuma) them, that is, tilts them, when flying. The meaning is: put it under your armpit. ﴿It will come out white﴾, with a radiance like the radiance of the sun that dazzles the sight, ﴿without harm﴾, that is, without leprosy, ﴿as another sign﴾ for your prophethood, white, and a sign; the two are circumstantial clauses together. "Without harm" is a complement of "white," as when you say, "it became white without harm." It is also permissible for "ayatan" (a sign) to be in the accusative by means of a deleted verb to which the lam [of purpose] is attached.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 23:

﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾. That is: take this sign too, after the turning of the staff into a serpent, so that with these two signs We may show you some of Our greatest, most magnificent signs; or, We may show you by means of them the greatest of Our signs. Or the meaning is: We did that so that We might show you of Our greatest signs.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 24:

﴿Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed.﴾ He exceeded the limit of servitude to the claim of lordship. And when He commanded him to go to the tyrannical Pharaoh, and he knew that he had been charged with a great matter that requires an expansive breast,

ﷺ

﴿He said: "My Lord, expand for me my breast"﴾ — i.e., widen it, so that it may bear the revelation, the hardships, and the ill manners of Pharaoh and his soldiers.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 26:

﴿And make my task easy for me﴾. Make easy for me what You commanded me of conveying the message to Pharaoh. "Expand for me my breast" is more emphatic than "Expand my breast," because it is a repetition of one meaning by way of summary (ijmal) and detail (tafsil). For by saying "Expand for me" and "make easy for me," it is known that there is something expanded and something made easy; then he removed the ambiguity by mentioning the breast and the task.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 27:

﴿And loosen﴾ open up, ﴿a knot from my tongue﴾. There was a speech impediment in his tongue due to the live coal that he had placed on his tongue in his childhood. That is because Musa (Moses) grabbed the beard of Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and slapped him with a severe slap while still a child, so he (Fir'awn) intended to kill him. Asiya said, "O King, he is a child and does not understand." So she placed fire in one basin and rubies in another basin and set them before Musa. He reached for the rubies, but the king moved his hand toward the fire, so he (Musa) lifted a live coal and placed it on his tongue, and his tongue was burned, so it became a lisp (lukna) from it. It is also related that his hand was burned, and Fir'awn exerted effort to treat it but it did not heal. When he (Musa) invited him, he (Fir'awn) said, "To which Lord are you calling me?" He (Musa) said, "To the One who heals my hand, which you have been unable to heal."

"From my tongue" is a description of "a knot," as if it were said: a knot from the knots of my tongue. This indicates that the knot had not entirely remained in its completeness, and most of them hold that all of it had gone.
﴿That they may understand my speech﴾ at the conveying of the message.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 29:

﴿And make for me a minister﴾ — a helper on whom I may rely. It is derived from al-wizr (الوِزْر), meaning burden, because he bears on behalf of the king his burdens and his responsibilities. Or it is derived from al-wazar (الوَزَر), meaning refuge, because the king takes shelter in his opinion and seeks refuge in him in his affairs. Or it is from al-mu'azarah (المُؤازَرَة), meaning assistance, which is mu'awanah (المُعاوَنَة), i.e. aid. So wazīran (وَزِيرًا) is the first object of ijʿal (اجْعَلْ), and the second is ﴿from my family﴾. Or, li (لِي) and wazīran are its two objects.

His saying ﴿Harun﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf al-bayān) to ﴿a minister﴾ (wazīran). His saying ﴿my brother﴾ is a substitute (badal) or another explicative apposition, or it is in apposition to ﴿a minister﴾ [Ṭāhā: 29]. ﴿Harun﴾ is its two objects, and the second of them was placed before the first out of concern for the matter of the ministry.
﴿Strengthen my back through him﴾. Make my back strong with him. It was also said that *al-أزْر* (al-azr) means strength.

{And associate him in my affair} — make him a partner of mine in prophethood and messengership. "Ashdud" and "wa-ushrikhu" are (read as) a report of the speaker's own words (in the first person): Ibn ʿAmir (al-Shamī) reads them as a response (to the previous request, i.e., in the form of a jussive answer), while the rest (of the readers) read them as a supplication and request.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 20, verse 33:

﴿That we may glorify You﴾: we pray to You and declare You free of every imperfection, with much tasbih (glorification of God).

﴿much﴾
﴿And that We may glorify You much﴾ in the prayers and outside them.
﴿Indeed You are ever Seeing of us﴾, knowing of our circumstances. So Allah, exalted is He, answered him, saying...

Allah said: ﴿He said, "You have been granted your request, O Moses."﴾ Meaning: you have been given what you asked for. Su'l (سُؤْل) means a request or petition; it is a form (fu'l) in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul), like khubz (خُبْز) meaning makhbuz (مَخْبُوز, "baked"). Abu 'Amr read "sūlaka" (سُولَكَ) without the hamza.
﴿And We had already bestowed favor upon you﴾ we conferred blessings (anʿamnā) ﴿another time﴾ an occasion (karra) ﴿before this﴾ before this one.

Then he explained it, saying: ﴿When We inspired in your mother that which is inspired﴾, by inspiration (ilhām) or by a dream, at the time you were born. Pharaoh used to kill the likes of you. And "idh" (when) is an adverbial complement (ẓarf) governed by "mananna" (We bestowed favour).

Then he explained what is inspired by His saying (p-364)

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 20, verse 39:**

﴿Cast him﴾ (*alqihi*), meaning: place him ﴿into the chest﴾ (*fi al-tabut*). *An* here is *mufassirah* (an explanatory particle, "that"), because the revelation (*al-wahy*) carries the sense of speech (*al-qawl*). ﴿So cast him into the river﴾ (*fi al-yamm*), meaning the Nile. ﴿Then let the river throw him onto the shore﴾ (*bi al-sahil*), meaning the bank. It is called *sahil* (shore) because the water *yasḥaluhu* (*yasḥal*: scrapes away, wears down) it, i.e., strips off its surface. The form is imperative to match what came before, but its meaning is informative: the river will cast him onto the shore. ﴿An enemy to Me and an enemy to him will take him﴾, meaning Pharaoh. All the pronouns refer back to Moses. Having some of them refer to Moses and others to the chest would lead to *tanabuz al-nazm* (disruption or clash in the arrangement of the verse), because the one cast into the sea and the one thrown onto the shore is the chest, although Moses was inside the chest.

It is narrated that she placed carded cotton in the chest, laid him in it, sealed it with pitch (*qayyarathu*), and then cast it into the river. A great canal ran from the river to Pharaoh's garden. While Pharaoh was sitting at the edge of a pool with Asiya, suddenly the chest appeared. He ordered it brought out and opened, and there was a boy, the most beautiful of people in face. Pharaoh loved him with a intense love. This is the meaning of His words: ﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾. *Minni* (from Me) is connected to *alqaytu* (I cast). The meaning is: "I made you beloved." Whomever God loves, hearts love, so no one saw him without loving him. Qatadah said: there was a radiance (*mulaha*) in Moses' eyes, so that no one saw him without loving him.

﴿And that you be raised﴾ (*wa litusna'a*) is coordinated with an omitted clause, whose estimated sense is: "and I cast upon you love, so that you would be loved, and so that you would be raised" ﴿under My eye﴾ (*'ala 'ayni*), meaning: so that you would be brought up within My sight. Its root is from *sana'a al-faras*, meaning he tended the horse well and cared for it. The meaning is: I watch over you and observe you, as a man watches over a thing with his own eye when he takes care of it.

"*Wa litus'na'*" (with the lam sukun and jazm) is read with the lam quiescent and in the jussive, meaning that it is in the imperative sense, as if He commanded it.

﴿When your sister walked along and said, "Shall I direct you to one who will take charge of him?"﴾ It is a substitution (*badal*) for "when We revealed," because her walking was a favour to him.

It is related that his sister Maryam came seeking news of him and found them looking for a wet-nurse for him, since he would accept no woman's breast. She said, (p-365) "Shall I direct you to one who will take him into her care and raise him?" She meant the wet-nurse by this. The verb is masculine because of the masculine form of "one" (*man*). They said, "Yes." So she brought his mother, and he accepted her breast. This is His saying, ﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾, that is, We gave you back to her, ﴿as We had promised her when We said, "We will return him to you"﴾ [al-Qasas: 7], ﴿that her eye might be comforted﴾ by meeting you, ﴿and that she should not grieve﴾ over your separation.

﴿And you killed a soul﴾, a Copt who was an unbeliever. ﴿Then We delivered you from distress﴾, that is, from retaliation (*qawad*). It is said that "distress" (*ghamm*) means killing in the dialect of Quraysh. It is also said that he was distressed because of the killing, fearing God's punishment and Pharaoh's retribution, and God forgave him through his seeking forgiveness. ﴿He said, "My Lord, I have wronged myself, so forgive me"﴾ [al-Qasas: 16]. He delivered him from Pharaoh by taking him away from Egypt to Madyan.

﴿And We tried you with a trial﴾, that is, We tested you by placing you in tribulations and rescuing you from them. *Futun* is a verbal noun like *qu'ud*, or the plural of *fitnah* (trial), meaning: We tried you with various kinds of trials. A *fitnah* is a tribulation, and everything with which God tests His servants is a *fitnah*. ﴿And We test you with evil and good as a trial﴾ [al-Anbiya: 35].

﴿Then you stayed years among the people of Madyan﴾. It is the town of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, eight stages from Egypt. Wahb said: he stayed with Shu'ayb for twenty-eight years, ten of which were the bridal gift (*mahr*) for Safura, and he remained with him eighteen years after that until children were born to him. ﴿Then you came at an appointed time, O Musa﴾, that is, at the appointed time and measure of the message, which was forty years.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 41:**

﴿And I have chosen you for Myself﴾: I chose you and selected you for My revelation and My message, so that you would act according to My will and My love. Al-Zajjaj said: "I chose you for My command, and I made you the one who establishes My proof (hujjah) and the one who speaks between Me and My creation, as if I had established the proof upon them and addressed them."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 42:

﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs﴾ with My miracles. ﴿And do not slacken﴾ do not become weak or lax, from al-wany (wanī), which is weakness (futur) and negligence (taqsir). ﴿in My remembrance﴾ meaning: take My remembrance as a wing with which you fly, or (p-366) by remembrance is meant the conveying of the message, for remembrance (dhikr) applies to all acts of worship, and conveying the message is among the greatest of them.

Translation:

﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh﴾ (He) repeated it because the first (command) is unrestricted (muṭlaq) and the second is restricted (muqayyad). ﴿Indeed, he has transgressed﴾ (jāwaza al-ḥadd): he exceeded the limit by claiming lordship (al-rubūbiyyah).

Speak to him gently: soften your speech to him, because of his right to have raised Moses, or address him by his kunya. He is one of those known by three kunyas: Abu al-Abbas, Abu al-Walid, and Abu Murra. Or [the gentle speech] means that He promised him youth that would never grow old and a kingdom that would not be taken from him except by death. Or it is his saying ﴿Would you like to purify yourself [of arrogance]?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 18] ﴿and I guide you to your Lord, so that you may fear Him?﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 19]. Its outward form is a question and a suggestion.

﴿Perhaps he will be mindful﴾, that is, he will take heed and reflect, and so submit to the truth. ﴿Or fear﴾, that is, he will fear that the matter is as you describe, and that his denial will lead him to ruin. He said "perhaps he will be mindful" while knowing that he would not be mindful, because the expectation (tarajji) belongs to the two of them: that is, go with your hope and your longing, and undertake the matter as one who hopes that his action will bear fruit. The benefit of sending them to him, despite knowing that he would not believe, is to establish the proof and cut off the excuse.

It was also said that its meaning is: perhaps someone who is mindful will be mindful, or someone who fears will fear, and this has happened among many people. It was also said that "perhaps" (la'alla) comes from Allah the Exalted, meaning it is binding, and he did become mindful, but only when mindfulness no longer benefited him. It was also said that Pharaoh did become mindful and feared, and wished to follow Moses, but Haman prevented him, for he would not decide any matter without him.

When this verse was recited before Yahya ibn Mu'adh, he wept and said: "This is your gentleness toward one who says, 'I am a god.' So how [will it be] toward one who says, 'You are the god'? And this is your gentleness toward one who says, 'I am your Lord, the Most High.' So how [will it be] toward one who says, 'Glory be to my Lord, the Most High'?"

"They said, 'Our Lord, we fear that he will hasten against us (with punishment), or that he will transgress (yatgha).'"

Here the verse is ﴿قالا رَبَّنا إنَّنا نَخافُ أنْ يَفْرُطَ عَلَيْنا أوْ أنْ يَطْغى﴾. The commentary explains that "yafruta 'alaynā" means he will hasten against us with punishment. From the same root comes al-fāriṭ (the forerunner, one who goes ahead), and it is said "faraṭa 'alayhi," meaning he hastened against him.

"Aw an yaṭghā" means he will exceed the limit in harming us.

﴿He said: "Do not fear. Indeed, I am with you both"﴾ meaning: I am your Guardian and your Helper. ﴿I hear﴾ your words ﴿and I see﴾ your deeds. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "I hear your supplication, so I respond to it, and I see what is intended against you, so I prevent it. I am not heedless of you, so do not worry."

﴿So go to him⦆ — that is, Pharaoh — ﴿and say: "Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord"⦆ to you — ﴿so send with us the Children of Israel⦆, that is, release them from enslavement and subjugation — ﴿and do not torment them⦆ by imposing hardships — ﴿We have come to you with a sign from your Lord⦆, a proof of the truth of what we claim. This sentence follows the first one, ﴿We are two messengers of your Lord⦆, serving as an elaboration and explanation, because the claim to prophethood is not established except by its evidence, which is the bringing of signs. So Pharaoh said, "And what is it?" Then he brought out his hand, and it had a radiance like the radiance of the sun. ﴿And peace is upon the one who follows the guidance⦆ — that is, whoever submits will be safe from punishment; and it is not a greeting. It was also said that it is the greeting of the angels, who are the guardians of Paradise, upon those who are guided.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 48:

﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment﴾ in this world and the Hereafter ﴿is upon whoever denies﴾ the Messengers ﴿and turns away﴾ (a'rada, i.e., turns away from faith). This is among the most hopeful verses of the Qur'an, because He made the category of peace for the believer and the category of punishment for the one who denies, and there is nothing beyond the category. So they (Moses and Aaron) came to him, delivered the message, and said to him what they had been commanded to say.

ـ﴿Qala faman Rabbukuma ya Musa﴾ — "He said: 'Who then is your Lord, O Musa?'" He addressed both of them, then called out to one of them, because Musa is the principal in prophethood and Harun is his follower.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 50:

﴿He said: Our Lord is He who gave everything its creation (khalqahu)﴾ "Khalqahu" is the first of the two objects of a'ta (gave): that is, He gave His creatures everything they need and from which they benefit. Or the second: that is, He gave everything its form and shape that corresponds to the benefit assigned to it, just as He gave the eye the configuration that corresponds to sight, and the ear the shape that suits hearing; likewise the nose, (p-368) the foot and the hand, each of them corresponds to the benefit assigned to it. Nusayr read "khalaqahu" as a qualifier either of the first noun in the construction or of the second: that is, He gave every created thing a gift. ﴿Then He guided﴾ He made known how to benefit from what He had given, for the sustenance of life in this world and for felicity in the world to come.

Pharaoh said, ﴿What then is the state of the former generations?﴾ That is, what is the condition of the bygone peoples and the decayed remains? He asked Moses about the state of those generations that had preceded, and about the wretchedness of those among them who were wretched and the happiness of those who were happy.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 52:

﴿Said﴾ Musa, answering: ﴿Its knowledge is with my Lord﴾. (ʿIlmuhā ʿindā rabbī) is a subject and predicate. "In a Book" (fī al-kitāb), that is, the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh), is a second predicate. That is: this is a question about the unseen, and Allah has reserved it for Himself; none knows it but Him. I am only a servant like you; I know of it only what the Knower of the unseen (ʿAllām al-Ghuyūb) has told me. The knowledge of the states of past generations is written with Allah in the Preserved Tablet. ﴿My Lord does not err﴾, that is, He does not make a mistake about anything. It is said: "ḍalaltu al-shayʾ" (I lost the thing) when you miss it in its place so that you do not find it. That is, He does not err concerning the happiness and misery of people. ﴿Nor does He forget﴾ their reward and their punishment. It has also been said: He does not forget what He has known, so that He would need to record it in the Book; rather, [the Book is recorded] so that the angels may know that what is produced in creation agrees with what is known to Him.

Alladhī (who) is in the nominative (marfūʿ) as a qualifier (ṣifah) of "my Lord," or as the predicate (khabar) of an omitted subject (mubtadaʾ), or it is in the accusative (manṣūb) by way of praise (madḥ): ﴿who made the earth for you a cradle﴾. The Kūfī reader and others read "mihādan," and both are dialectal forms (lughatān) for that which spreads out and lays flat. ﴿And threaded﴾, i.e., made, ﴿for you therein roads﴾, paths. ﴿And sent down from the sky water﴾, i.e., rain, ﴿and We brought forth by it﴾, by the water. The speech shifts from the third person (ghaybah) to the first-person speaker (mutakallim), in conformity with the variation of style (iftinān). It was also said that Moses' speech ended there, and then God Most High informed about Himself with His words ﴿and We brought forth by it﴾. It was also said that this is the speech of Moses, i.e., "so We brought forth," meaning We Ourselves, by tilling and planting. ﴿Kinds﴾, i.e., varieties, ﴿of plants﴾. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) by which the plant (nabāt) is named, so the singular and plural are alike in it. ﴿Diverse﴾ is an attribute of "kinds" or of "plants," the plural of shatīt, like marīḍ and marḍā. That is, they differ in benefit, color, smell and form: some are for people and some are for animals. Among the blessings of God Most High is that our provision is obtained through the labor of livestock, and God has made their fodder from what exceeds our need, from that which we cannot eat, saying. (p-369)

Eat and let your cattle graze (﴿كُلُوا وارْعَوْا أنْعامَكُمْ﴾). It is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in "fa-akhrajnā" (so We brought forth). The meaning is: We brought forth various kinds of vegetation, permitting you to benefit from them, allowing you to eat some of them and to feed some of them to your livestock. (﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ﴾) In that, i.e., in what I have mentioned, (﴿لآياتٍ﴾) there are signs, i.e., proofs (dalālāt), (﴿لأُولِي النُهى﴾) for those possessing intellects. Its singular is nuhya (نُهْيَة), because it restrains (tanhā) one from what is forbidden, or because people come to a conclusion (yuntahā ilayhā) in matters through it.

"From it We created you" — from the earth; that is, your father Adam, peace be upon him. It was also said: He kneads every drop of semen with some dust from its burial place, so that one is created from both the dust and the semen together. Or it is because semen comes from food, and food comes from the earth.

"And into it We will return you" — when you die and are buried.

"And from it We will bring you out" — at the Resurrection, "a second time" (tāratan ukhrā), meaning another time. What is meant by bringing them out is that He will reassemble their scattered parts that are mixed with the dust, return them as they were when alive, and bring them out to the place of gathering.

Allah enumerated for them the benefits of the earth that are connected to them, in that He made it a bed and a cradle for them, on which they turn about. He also laid out in it pathways in which they travel as they wish. He caused to grow in it the kinds of plants from which are their sustenance and the fodder of their livestock. It is their origin from which they branched out, and their mother from which they were born, and it is their receptacle when they die.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 56:

﴿And We certainly showed him﴾, that is, Pharaoh, ﴿Our signs, all of them﴾. They were nine signs: the staff, the hand, the splitting of the sea, the stone, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, and the lifting of the mountain (natq al-jabal). ﴿But he denied﴾ the signs ﴿and refused﴾ to accept the truth.

Pharaoh said: ﴿Have you come to us to drive us out of our land﴾, Egypt, ﴿with your magic, O Moses?﴾ In this there is evidence that he feared him greatly. His saying "with your magic" is a pretext (ta'allul); otherwise, what sorcerer could have the power to drive a king out of his land?!

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 58:

﴿So we will surely bring you [such] magic like it.﴾ That is: "we will surely oppose you with magic like your magic." ﴿So set up between us and you an appointment﴾ (mawʿid) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the sense of a promise (al-waʿd), and a noun governing a genitive is understood, i.e., "a place of appointment." The pronoun in ﴿we will not fail it﴾ refers to the appointment (al-mawʿid). Yazid read it with jazm (lā nukhlifhu), as a response to the imperative (jawāb al-amr), while others read it with raf‘ (lā nukhlifuhu), as a descriptive clause (waṣf) for the appointment. ﴿Neither we nor you [shall fail it] at a place﴾ (makānan) is a substitute (badal) for the omitted place-noun. It is also permissible that no noun governing a genitive be understood, and the meaning would be: "Set up between us and you a promise which we will not fail," and makānan is in the accusative by the verbal noun or by a verb indicated by the verbal noun. ﴿Equitable (suwan)﴾ with kasra is the reading of the Hijazis, Abu ʿAmr and ʿAli; the others read it with ḍamma. It is a qualifier (naʿt) of makānan, i.e., "an equitable place between us and you," and it derives from istiwāʾ (evenness), because the distance from the middle to both extremes is equal.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 59:

﴿Said he: "Your appointment is the Day of Adornment"﴾ is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate). It refers to a festival day that they had, or the Day of Nawruz (Nawruz, the Persian New Year), or the Day of 'Ashura' (the tenth of Muharram). The answer was given in terms of time, even though the question concerned place, according to the interpretation of the first option, because their gathering on the Day of Adornment would necessarily take place in some place; by mentioning the time, the place becomes known. On the second option, its estimate is: "Your promise is the promise of the Day of Adornment." ﴿And that the people be gathered﴾, i.e., be assembled, is in a position of raf' (nominative) or jarr (genitive) by way of 'atf (conjunction) upon "day" or "Adornment." ﴿In the forenoon﴾, i.e., at the time of mid-morning, so that it would be farther from suspicion, clearer for disclosing the truth, and so that it would spread among all the people of the camel-hair tents and the town dwellers.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 60:**

﴿So Pharaoh turned away﴾: he withdrew from Musa, turning away from him. ﴿Then he gathered his guile﴾: his scheming and his sorcerers. They numbered seventy-two, or four hundred, or seventy thousand. ﴿Then he came﴾ to the appointed time.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 61:

﴿Musa said to them﴾: that is, to the sorcerers. ﴿Woe to you! Do not fabricate a lie against Allah, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾: do not call His signs and miracles sorcery. ﴿Fa-yushhitakum﴾ (lest He destroy you): Kufan readers other than Abu Bakr read it as "yuhlikakum" (He will destroy you), and others read it with a fatha on the ya and the ha. Al-suht (ruin) and al-is-hat (annihilation) have the same meaning, namely annihilation. It is in the accusative because it is an answer to the prohibition (jawab al-nahy, the response following a negative command). ﴿with a punishment﴾: a great one. ﴿And he has indeed failed who fabricates﴾: whoever lies against Allah. (p-371)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 62:

﴿So they disputed their affair among themselves⦅فَتَنازَعُوا⦆﴾ — they differed (ikhtalafu), that is, the magicians. Some of them said, "This is a magician like us," and others said, "This is not the speech of magicians," that is: ﴿Do not invent a lie against Allah, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61], the verse. ﴿They conferred privately among themselves and kept their counsel secret﴾, that is, they consulted in secret and said, "If he is a magician, we will overcome him; and if he is from the heaven, then he has a command." The word najwa (secret counsel) may be used as a verbal noun (masdar) and as a noun (ism). Then they fabricated this speech, meaning:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 63:

﴿They said: Indeed these two are certainly sorcerers﴾ meaning: Musa and Harun. Abu 'Amr recited: "Inna hadhayni la-sahiran" (إنَّ هَذَيْنِ لَساحِرانِ), and this is apparent, but it contradicts the reading of al-Imam (Ibn 'Amir), Ibn Kathir, Hafs, and al-Khalil, who is more knowledgeable in grammar (nahw) and lexicography (lughah). ﴿Inna hadhani la-sahiran﴾ with the "inna" lightened (takhfif), like your saying: in Zayd la-munTaliq (إنْ زَيْدٌ لَمُنْطَلِقٌ). The lam is the one that distinguishes the negative "in" (إنْ النافِيَةِ) from the lightened form of the heavy "inna" (المُخَفَّفَةِ مِنَ الثَقِيلَةِ). It has also been said that "in" here has the meaning of "ma" (ما), and the lam has the meaning of "illa" (إلّا), i.e., "ma hadhani illa sahiran." Its evidence is the reading of Ubayy: "In dhani illa sahiran" (إنْ ذانِ إلّا ساحِرانِ). Others read "Inna hadhani la-sahiran." It has been said that this is the dialect of Bal-Harith ibn Ka'b, Khath'am, Murad, and Kinanah, for in their dialect the dual is always with an alif, so they did not convert it to a ya' in the genitive and accusative, like 'asa (عَصًا) and Su'da (سُعْدى). He said:

"Inna abaha wa-aba abaha qad balaghaa / fi al-majdi ghayataha"

Al-Zajjaj said: "inna" here means "na'am" (نَعَمْ, yes). The poet said:

"wa-yaqulna shaybun qad 'ala-ka wa-qad kabirta / faqultu innahu"

i.e., "na'am" (yes). The ha' is for pausal stopping (lil-waqf). "Hadhani" is the subject (mubtada'), and "sahiran" is the predicate (khabar) of an elided subject, and the lam enters upon the elided subject; its estimated form is: "hadhani lahuma sahiran," so the lam's entry is in its proper place, which is the beginning (ibtida'). Or the lam may enter the predicate just as it enters the subject. He said:

"khali la-anta wa-man Jarir khaluhu / ......"

[He said:] "I presented it to al-Mubarrad and he approved of it, though Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) rejected it."

﴿They wish to drive you out of your land﴾, Egypt, ﴿by their magic, and to take away your ideal way﴾ — your religion and your law — ﴿al-muthla﴾, the most excellent. It is the feminine of al-amthal, which means the most excellent.

**[Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 64]**

﴿So gather your scheme﴾, that is, make it firm. That is: make it something agreed upon, so that you do not differ. «Fa-jmaʿū» is the reading of Abu ʿAmr, and it is supported by «fa-jamaʿa kaydahu» (20:60). «Kayadihim» (a variant reading) refers to what is used for scheming. ﴿Then come forward in ranks﴾: «muṣṭaffīna» (lined up in rows) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) clause. They were commanded to come in a row, because it is more awe-inspiring in the hearts of the onlookers. ﴿And whoever prevails today has indeed succeeded﴾: whoever prevails has won. This is an iʿtirāḍ (parenthetical clause).

"They said": that is, the magicians said, "O Moses, either you throw [your staff] first, or we will be the first to throw what is with us."

The position of "an" (that) together with what follows it in both places is either in the accusative, governed by a verb understood, or in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: choose one of the two matters, or the matter is your throwing or our throwing. This offer of choice from them is an instance of good manners toward him. It is as if God inspired them with this, and He had conveyed His blessing to them, and He taught Moses to choose that they throw first, until

"He said: Nay, throw [first]," — that is, you throw first — "so that they may display what they have of the tricks of magic, and so that Allah may manifest His authority, and cast the truth upon falsehood so that it crushes it, and make the miracle prevail over the magicians so that it annihilates it, and so it becomes a clear sign for those who look and a manifest lesson for those who take heed." So they threw, ﴿and behold, their ropes and their staffs﴾. It is said that in ﴿إذا﴾ (idha) here is the "idha" of sudden occurrence (al-mufajaʾa). The verified view, however, is that it is the idha that denotes time (al-kaʾina bi-ma'na al-waqt), which requires a verb as its governor (nasib) and a clause that is added to it; in some contexts it is restricted to the case where its governor is a specific verb, namely the verb of suddenness (fiʿl al-mufajaʾa), and the clause following it is a nominal clause (ibtida'iyya) and nothing else. The estimated sense is: "fa-fajaʾa Musa waqt takhayyuli saʿy hibalihim wa-ʿisiyyihim" (then Musa was suddenly confronted at the moment of the imagining of the movement of their ropes and staffs). The meaning is: at his sudden encounter with their ropes and staffs, which made him imagine that they were moving.

﴿yukhayyalu﴾ (it seemed) — and with the ta' (tukhayyalu) according to Ibn Dhakwan — ﴿ilayhi﴾ (to him), that is, to Musa, ﴿min sihrihim annaha tasʿa﴾ (because of their magic, that they were moving). It is in the nominative case as a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the pronoun in yukhayyalu, meaning: the one who casts (the illusion) makes it seem. It is related that they had smeared them with mercury, and when the sun struck them they began to tremble and move, and so this created that appearance.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself﴾

He concealed within himself a fear, supposing that they (the ropes and staffs) were aimed at him, owing to the human nature (jibillah bashariyyah), or he feared that doubt would creep into the people's minds so that they would not follow him.

"We said: Do not fear; indeed you are the Most High" (﴿قُلْنا لا تَخَفْ إنَّكَ أنْتَ الأعْلى﴾). Al-A'la (al-A'la): the dominant, the one who overpowers.

In the mention of inna (indeed), anta (you, emphatic pronoun), the definite article (harf al-ta'rif), and the word al-'uluww (highness), which means manifest dominance, there is a clear emphasis (mubalaghah).

Recited with a sukun (the vowelless mark) on the lam and the fa, and with the qaf lightened: Hafs (the transmitter Hafs) reads it so, while Ibn Dhakwan reads "tulaqqafu" (with the first verb form in the passive-causative pattern, lightened qaf), and the rest read "talaqqaf" (with the qaf doubled).

﴿ma ṣana'ū﴾ (what they have made) means zawwarū wa-if'talū (they forged and fabricated). That is, throw down your staff, and it will swallow up their staffs and ropes. It does not say "your staff" out of exalting it, meaning: do not be impressed by what they have made, for what is in your right hand is greater than it. Or it is said out of belittling them, meaning: do not be concerned with the multitude of their ropes and staffs, but throw the single, lone stick that is in your right hand, for by Our power it will swallow them, despite its oneness and their multitude.

﴿Innamā ṣana'ū kaydu sāḥirin﴾ (what they have made is only the trick of a magician). The Kufan reading "siḥrin" (of sorcery) without ʿĀṣim's reading means "possessed of sorcery." Or, because of their deep immersion in sorcery, they themselves are as if they were sorcery. "Kaydu" is in the nominative in both readings. "Mā" is either a relative pronoun (mawṣūla) or a verbal-infinitive particle (maṣdariyya). "Sāḥir" is kept singular and not made plural, because the intention in this statement is the sense of kind (jinsiyya, the category as a whole) and not the sense of number. Had it been pluralized, it would have been imagined that the intended meaning is a count. Do you not see His saying: ﴿and the magician does not prosper﴾, meaning this kind of person, ﴿wherever he goes﴾ (ḥaythu atā), wherever he may be.

So Mūsā threw his staff, and it swallowed up what they had made. Because of the great sign they had witnessed, they were pushed down into prostration. That is His saying:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 70:

﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate.﴾ Al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat, a grammarian) said: "Because of the speed with which they prostrated, it is as if they had been thrown down. How remarkable their situation! They threw down their ropes and staffs for disbelief and denial, then after an hour they threw down their heads in thanks and prostration. How great is the difference between the two casting-downs!" It is related that they saw the Garden and their places in it while they were prostrate, so they raised their heads [and] then ﴿said: "We believe in the Lord of Aaron and Moses."﴾ He mentioned Aaron first here and later in al-Shu'ara' (the Poets) [he mentioned him second], in observance of the rhyme (fasila), and because the conjunction "wa" (and) does not necessarily imply order (tartib).

Al-Nasafi, *Madarik al-Tanzil*, on Surah 20, verse 71:

﴿He said, "Have you believed in him before I gave you permission?"﴾ Ḥafṣ reads ﴿آمَنتُمْ﴾ without the elongation (*madd*, the lengthening of a vowel). Al-Baṣrī, al-Shāmī and al-Ḥijāzī read it with an elongated hamza, and others read it with two hamzas. ﴿لَهُ قَبْلَ أنْ آذَنَ لَكُمْ﴾ means: to Mūsā. It is said *āmana lahu* and *āmana bihi*, both meaning "he believed in him." ﴿Indeed, he is your chief (*kabīrukum*) who taught you magic.﴾ That is, your greatest or your teacher. The people of Makkah would say to the teacher, "My *kabīr* ordered me," meaning his senior or master. ﴿So I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides.﴾ Cutting "from opposite sides" means cutting the right hand and the left foot, because each of the two limbs differs from the other: this is a hand and that is a foot, and this is the right side and that is the left. The *min* in ﴿مِن خِلافٍ﴾ is *min* of the beginning of the end-point (*min li-ibtidā' al-ghāyah*), because the cutting begins from and arises from one limb differing from the other. The grammatical position of the prepositional phrase *min khilāf* is accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*ḥāl*), meaning: I will cut them off while they are differing from one another, because when some of them differ from others, they are characterized by difference. The fixing of the crucified man in the trunk is likened to the fixing of a contained object in its container, and therefore He said: ﴿and I will surely crucify you on the trunks of palm trees.﴾ The palm tree is specified because its trunks are long. ﴿And you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment﴾: I, on account of your belief in him, or the Lord of Mūsā, on account of your abandoning belief. It is also said that he means himself, may God curse him, and Mūsā, may the blessings and peace of God be upon him, on the evidence of his saying ﴿Have you believed in him?﴾ The preposition *lām* with the verb *āmana* in the Book of God is used for other than God, as in His saying ﴿He believes in God and believes for (*yu'minu lil-mu'minīn*) the believers﴾ [al-Tawbah: 61]. ﴿And more enduring﴾: more lasting.

ِ﴿They said, "We will not prefer you over what has come to us of the clear proofs"﴾ — لَنْ نَخْتارَكَ, we will not choose you — ﴿over what has come to us of the clear proofs﴾ — القاطِعَةِ, the decisive ones, الدالَّةِ عَلى صِدْقِ مُوسى, indicating the truthfulness of Musa (ʿalayhi al-salam) — ﴿and over Him who originated us﴾ — عَطْفٌ عَلى ما جاءَنا, a conjunction with "what has come to us"; i.e., we will not choose you over what has come to us, nor over Him who created us. Or it is an oath, and its answer is ﴿We will not prefer you﴾, which is placed before the oath.

﴿So decree what you will decree﴾ — فاصْنَعْ ما أنْتَ صانِعٌ, do what you will do, of cutting and crucifying. (p-375) Al-Nasafi cites: "and upon them both are chain-mail coats, which he decreed (qadāhumā)", i.e., he made them. Or: احْكم ما أنْتَ حاكِمٌ, judge what you will judge.

﴿You can only decree concerning this worldly life﴾ — أيْ: في هَذِهِ الحَياةِ الدُنْيا, i.e., in this worldly life, so الدُنْيا is in the accusative as an adverb of time (ẓarf). That is: you can only judge concerning us for the duration of our life.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 73:

﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the magic to which you compelled us.﴾ "Mā" is a relative pronoun in the accusative, governed by conjunction (ʿaṭf) with "khaṭāyānā" (our sins). ﴿min al-siḥr﴾ (from magic) is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to "mā." It is narrated that they said to Pharaoh: "Show us Moses asleep." He did so, and they found him, and his staff was guarding him. So they said: "This is not magic, for when a magician sleeps, his magic ceases to work." They disliked opposing him for fear of disgrace, so Pharaoh compelled them to produce the magic. Observe how their knowledge of magic benefited them, while Pharaoh's ignorance of it harmed him. Then how much more so with the knowledge of the Sharia (Islamic law)?!

﴿And Allah is better﴾ in reward for those who obey Him ﴿and more enduring﴾ in punishment for those who disobey Him. This is a refutation of Pharaoh's words: ﴿And you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more enduring﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 71].

"Innahu" here is the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-sha'n, the pronoun of the matter/situation). ﴿Whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal (mujrimān)﴾, meaning an unbeliever, ﴿then for him﴾, that is, for the criminal, ﴿is Hell; he will neither die therein﴾, so that he would find rest through death, ﴿nor will he live﴾ a life from which he would benefit.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 75:

﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer﴾ — that is, dies upon faith. ﴿Having done righteous deeds﴾ — after faith. ﴿For them are the high ranks﴾ — al-'ulā is the plural of al-'ulyā (the feminine of the superlative "highest").

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 76:

﴿Gardens of Eden﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the high ranks," ﴿beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾, meaning remaining eternally, ﴿and that is the reward of him who purifies himself﴾, meaning he who cleanses himself of shirk by his saying "There is no god but Allah." It has been said that these three verses are a quotation of their words (hikaya), and it has been said that it is a report from Allah the Exalted, not in the manner of quotation, and this is the more apparent (azhar).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 77:

﴿And We revealed to Musa: "Travel by night with My servants."﴾ When Allah the Exalted willed to destroy Fir'awn (Pharaoh) and his people, He commanded Musa to depart with them from Misr (Egypt) by night and to take them along the way of the sea. ﴿So strike for them a dry path in the sea.﴾ Ijʿal lahum (make for them): from their saying, ḍaraba lahu fī mālihi sahman (he set for him a share in his wealth). ﴿Dry (yabasan)﴾ meaning: dry. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as an adjective; one says yabisa yabasan wa-yubsan. ﴿Fear not (lā takhāfu)﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the pronoun in fāḍrib, meaning: strike for them a path, not fearing. Ḥamzah reads "lā takhaf" in apocopate form as a response (jawāb) to the command. ﴿Overtaken (darakan)﴾ is a noun from the verb "to overtake" (al-idrāk), meaning: Fir'awn and his hosts will not overtake you, nor reach you. ﴿Nor fear (wa-lā takhsha)﴾ drowning. According to Ḥamzah's reading "wa-lā takhsha" it is a resumptive clause (isti'nāf), meaning: "and you do not fear." Or the alif is for extension (iṭlāq), as in ﴿And you entertain thoughts about Allah﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 10]. So Musa departed with them at the beginning of the night, and they were seventy thousand. They had borrowed their jewelry, and Fir'awn set out with six hundred thousand of the Copts, and he followed their track. That is His saying.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 78:

﴿So Pharaoh followed them with his hosts﴾, and this is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: he went out after them, and his hosts were with him. ﴿So the sea covered them, that which covered them﴾, meaning: what struck them from the sea. ﴿That which covered them﴾ is one of the comprehensive expressions (jawami' al-kalim) which, though few in words, carry many meanings; meaning: there covered them that whose reality none knows except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 79:

﴿And Pharaoh led his people astray﴾ from the path of right guidance, ﴿and did not guide them﴾, that is, he did not direct them to the truth and rectitude. This is a refutation of his statement: ﴿And I only show you the path of right guidance﴾ [Ghafir: 29].

Then He recounted His favor upon the Children of Israel after He had delivered them from the sea and destroyed Pharaoh and his people, by saying: ﴿O Children of Israel﴾, meaning: We revealed to Musa, "Travel by night with My servants," and We said, "O Children of Israel, ﴿We have delivered you from your enemy﴾," meaning Pharaoh, ﴿and We made a covenant with you﴾ to give you the Book ﴿at the right side of the Mount﴾. This was because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, promised Musa that he would come to this place and choose seventy men who would attend him for the descent of the Torah. The covenant (mu'adah) was attributed to them, because it was made with their prophet and their chiefs (nuqaba'), and its benefits returned to them, since their law (shar') and religion (din) were established by it. The word "al-ayman" (the right) is in the accusative case (nasb), because it is an attribute (sifah) of "janib" (side). It was also read in the genitive (jarr) by virtue of proximity (al-jiwar). ﴿And We sent down upon you the manna and the quail﴾ in the wilderness (al-tih), and We said to you...

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 81:

﴿Eat of the good things﴾ (ṭayyibāt), meaning lawful (ḥalālāt), ﴿with which We have provided you﴾, meaning: "We have delivered you, promised you, and provided for you." This is the reading of Kūfī (the Kufan readers) other than ʿĀṣim. ﴿And do not transgress therein﴾, meaning: do not exceed the limits of Allah therein, by being ungrateful for the blessings and spending them in acts of disobedience; or [it means]: let none of you wrong another. ﴿Lest My wrath descend upon you﴾, meaning My punishment. ﴿And whoever has My wrath descend upon him has indeed perished﴾, meaning he has been destroyed, or has fallen in a fall from which there is no rising. ʿAlī read "fayaḥul" (﴿فَيَحُلَّ﴾) and "yaḥlul" (﴿يَحْلُلْ﴾), while the rest read both with a kasra. The form with kasra carries the meaning of obligation, from ḥalla al-dayn (ḥalla al-dayn yaḥillu), meaning the debt became due when its payment became obligatory. The form with ḍamma carries the meaning of descending.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 82:

﴿And indeed, I am Most Forgiving toward one who repents﴾ from polytheism (al-shirk), ﴿and believes﴾ affirms the oneness of God, exalted is He, and confirms what He has sent down, ﴿and does righteous work﴾ performs the obligatory duties (al-fara'id), ﴿then remains guided﴾ then remains upright and stays firm upon guidance (al-huda), and this is repentance, faith, and righteous work.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 83:

﴿And what hastened you away﴾ from your people, O Musa? That is: what thing hastened you away ﴿from your people, O Musa﴾, that is, from the seventy whom he had chosen. The reason is that he set out with them toward Mount Tur at the appointed time, then went ahead of them out of longing for the speech of his Lord, and he commanded them to follow him. So Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And what hastened you away﴾, that is: what thing necessitated your haste? It is an interrogative of disapproval (istifham inkar), and "ma" is the subject (mubtada'), and "a'jalaka" (hastened you) is the predicate (khabar).

He said, ﴿They are right behind me on my track.﴾ That is, they are behind me, following me, and there is only a short distance between me and them. Then he mentioned the reason for his haste and said, ﴿And I hastened to You, my Lord,﴾ that is, to the appointment You promised, ﴿that You may be pleased.﴾ That You may increase in being pleased with me. This is evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) (p-378).

"He said, 'Indeed We have tested your people after you.'" We put them into trial after you, after your departure from among them. By "the people" is meant those whom you left behind with Harun. "And the Samiri has led them astray" through his calling them to the worship of the calf and their response to him. He is ascribed to a tribe of the Children of Israel called the Samirah. It was also said that he was a foreigner (ʿilj) from Kerman, who made a calf. His name was Musa ibn Zafar, and he was a hypocrite (munafiq).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 86:

﴿So Musa returned﴾ from his intimate conversation with his Lord, ﴿to his people, angry and grieved﴾, i.e., extremely angry, or sorrowful. ﴿He said: "O my people, did your Lord not make you a good promise?"﴾ God had promised them that He would give them the Torah, in which there is guidance and light, and it consisted of a thousand surahs, each surah of a thousand verses, and seventy camels would carry its books. There is no promise better than that. ﴿"Has the period (al-ahd) seemed long to you?"﴾ That is: the length of my absence from you. Al-ahd means time; it is said, "Ṭāla ʿahdī bika" (my time with you has been long), meaning my time has become long because of your separation from you. ﴿"Or did you desire that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?"﴾ That is: did you desire to do an action that would make wrath from your Lord obligatory upon you? ﴿"So you broke your promise to me."﴾ They had promised him that they would remain upon his command, and that he had left them with the signs, but they broke their promise to him by taking the calf.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on Surah 20, verse 87:

﴿They said: "We did not break our promise to you of our own power."﴾ With a fatha on the *mim* (*bi-fathi al-mim*, *maliknā*), it is read by Madani and ʿAsim; with a damma (*bi-ḍammihā*), by Hamzah and ʿAli; and with a kasra (*bi-kasrihā*), by the others. The meaning is: "We did not break our promise to you by means of having power over our affair." That is, "Had we been in control of our affair and left to our own judgement, we would not have broken our promise to you. But we were overpowered by the Samiri and his scheming." ﴿But we were loaded﴾ with a damma and a shadda (*bi-ḍ-ḍamm wa-t-tashdīd*) is read by the Hijazi and Shami and Hafs; with a fatha on the *ḥāʾ* and *mīm* and without shadda, by the others. ﴿with burdens of the people's ornaments﴾: loads of the jewellery of the Copts. Or they meant by "burdens" that they were sins and consequences, because they had borrowed the ornaments on the night of the departure from Egypt, under the pretext that "tomorrow is a festival for us." Then the Samiri said: "Musa was only delayed because of the ill-omen of the (unlawful) taking of these." For they were, with them, in the legal status of *mustaʾmanīn* (those granted safe-conduct, i.e. protected non-combatants) in *dār al-ḥarb* (the territory of war), and it is not lawful for one granted safe-conduct to take the property of the *ḥarbī* (a combatant of the enemy). Moreover, the spoils of war were not lawful at that time. So they burned them. Then he (the Samiri) hid in the pit of the fire the mould of a calf, and it was cast as a hollow calf, and it lowed by the entry of the wind into channels in it resembling veins. It was also said that he blew into it dust from the place of the hooves of Jibril's horse on the day of the drowning, and it was the horse of life, so it came alive and lowed. Their natures inclined towards gold, so they worshipped it.

﴿So I threw it﴾ into the Samiri's fire which he had kindled in the pit, and we were commanded to cast the ornaments into it. ﴿Thus did the Samiri cast﴾ what he had of the ornaments into the fire, or what he had of the dust which he had taken from the imprint of the hoof of Jibril's horse, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (*Madarik al-Tanzil*) on surah 20, verse 88:

﴿So he brought forth for them﴾ al-Samiri from the pit ﴿a calf﴾, which Allah created from the ornaments that the fire had melted, as a trial. ﴿A body﴾ embodied, ﴿having a lowing﴾, meaning a sound. It used to low as young calves low. ﴿Then they said﴾, that is, al-Samiri and his followers, ﴿This is your god and the god of Musa﴾. Most of them responded to him, except twelve thousand. ﴿But he forgot﴾, meaning Musa forgot his Lord here and went to seek Him at the Tur. Or it is the beginning of a statement from Allah the Exalted, meaning: al-Samiri forgot his Lord and abandoned the outward faith he had held. Or: al-Samiri forgot the reasoning that a calf cannot be a god, as is shown by His saying

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 89:

﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them a word﴾ meaning: that it does not return. Here "an" (أنَّ) is the lightened form (mukhaffafah) of the heavy "inna" (al-thaqilah). ﴿Nor does it have power to harm them or benefit them﴾ meaning: it is incapable of speech, of harm, and of benefit, so how can you take it as a god? It is also said that it lowed (khara) only once.

﴿And indeed Harun had said to them﴾ to those who worshipped the calf, ﴿before [this], from before Musa returned to them: "O my people, you are only being tested by it"﴾ meaning you have been tried with the calf, so do not worship it. ﴿And indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful﴾ not the calf. ﴿So follow me﴾ be upon my religion, which is the truth. ﴿And obey my command﴾ in abandoning the worship of the calf. (p-380)

"They said, 'We will not cease to be devoted to it (in worship) until Musa returns to us,' that is: we will not stop remaining upon the calf and its worship, ﴿until Musa returns to us﴾, so that we may see him: whether he will worship it as we have worshipped it, and whether al-Samiri spoke the truth or not. So when Musa returned..."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 92:

﴿He said: "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray,"﴾ by worshipping the calf.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 93:

﴿Why did you not follow me?﴾ With the yā' (ya) in both continuation and pause, Makkī (Ibn Kathīr) read it, and Abū ʿAmr and Nāfiʿ agreed with him in continuation; the others read it without yā'. Meaning: what prompted you not to follow me, given that there is a connection between that which turns one away from doing something and that which calls one to leave it? It is also said that lā is extra (ṣilah), and the meaning is: what prevented you from following me when they did not accept your word, and joining me and informing me? Or: what prevented you from following me in anger for God? And why did you not fight those who disbelieved with those who believed? And why did you not, as I would have done had I been present, take up the matter yourself?

﴿So have you disobeyed my command?﴾ That is, the command I gave you concerning caring for their welfare. Then he seized his brother's head by his right hand and his beard by his left, in anger and in rebuke of him, because zeal for God had overcome him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 94:

﴿He said: "O son of my mother!"﴾ Reading the mim with a kasra (ibn Umm) is the reading of al-Shami and al-Kufi, except Hafs. He had a full brother and sister through both parents according to the majority (of scholars). But he mentioned the mother to elicit compassion and softening (of heart). ﴿"Do not seize me by my beard or by my head."﴾ Then he stated his excuse, saying: ﴿"Indeed, I feared that you would say"﴾ that "you have caused division among the Children of Israel" if I fought some of them against others. Or (it means): I feared that if I separated from them and followed you, a group would join me and another group would follow the Samiri, and you would say, "You have caused division among the Children of Israel." ﴿"And you did not observe"﴾ and did not keep in mind ﴿"my word."﴾ (That is,) "Take my place among my people and set things right." In this there is evidence for the permissibility of ijtihad (independent reasoning, exertion of judgment).
Then Musa turned to the Samiri, rebuking him, and said: ﴿What is your business, O Samiri?﴾ — that is, what is your matter, the affair about which you are being addressed?

"Said he: 'I perceived what they did not perceive; so I took a handful from the footprint of the Messenger, and cast it.'" 

Wait, I must translate the full passage faithfully. Here is the translation:

﴿He said: "I saw what they did not see﴾. [The verb] with the taa' is read by Hamzah and ʿAli. Al-Zajjaj said: basura means "he knew," and abṣara means "he looked." That is: "I knew what they did not know, the Children of Israel." Musa said: "And what is that?" He said: "I saw Jibril upon the horse of life, so it was cast into my soul that I should take a handful from its track. So whatever I cast upon anything, it became living, having spirit, flesh and blood." ﴿So I took a handful﴾. The qabḍah is one grasp from the verb qabaḍa, and applying it to what is grasped is naming the object by the verbal noun, like "the ruler's striking" (ḍarb al-amīr). It is also read "faqabaṣtu qabṣah," where the ḍād means with the whole palm and the ṣād with the fingertips. ﴿From the footprint of the Messenger﴾, that is, from the footprint of the Messenger's horse; and it is read with this variant. ﴿Then I cast it﴾, that is, I threw it into the hollow of the calf. ﴿And thus my soul enticed me﴾, that is, adorned it for me, to do it, so I did it, following my desire. This is an acknowledgment of error and an apology for it.

﴿He said﴾ to him, Moses: ﴿"Then go"﴾ from among us, an outcast. ﴿"Indeed, for you in this life"﴾ is [this] for as long as you live: ﴿"that you will say"﴾ to anyone who wants to mix with you, not knowing your condition, ﴿"No touching"﴾. That is: no one may touch me, and I may not touch him. Thus he was prevented from all mixing with people, and it was forbidden for them to meet him, speak with him, or trade with him. If it happened that someone touched him, both the toucher and the one touched would be struck with fever. He would wander in the desert shouting, "No touching." It is said that this condition persists in his descendants until now. It was also said that Moses, peace be upon him, wanted to kill him, but God the Exalted prevented him from doing so because of his generosity. ﴿"And indeed, for you there is a appointed time you will not be able to break"﴾. That is: God will not break for you His appointment that He promised you for [your] polytheism and corruption on earth. He will fulfill it for you in the Hereafter, after He has punished you for that in this world. The reading ﴿"you will not break it"﴾ (لَنْ تُخْلِفَهُ) is that of Makki and Abu 'Amr, and it comes from أُخْلِفْتُ المَوْعِدَ, meaning "I found the appointment to be broken," i.e., I found that it had not been kept. ﴿"And look at your god to which you remained devoted"﴾. The original form is ظَلِلْتَ, and the first lām was deleted for ease of pronunciation (تَخْفِيفًا). ﴿"Devoted"﴾: staying [there], remaining. ﴿"We will surely burn it"﴾ with fire, ﴿"then we will surely scatter it"﴾, that is, we will winnow it, ﴿"into the sea, dispersing [it]"﴾. So he burned it and scattered it into the sea. Some of them drank from its water out of love for it, and as a result the yellow of gold appeared on their lips. (p-382)

﴿Indeed, your god is only Allah, other than whom there is no deity, and He has encompassed all things in knowledge.﴾ [It is] a specification (tamyiz): that is, His knowledge has encompassed all things.

The place of the kaf in ﴿kadhalika﴾ is in the accusative, meaning: "Just as We have related to you the story of Moses and Pharaoh, ﴿We relate to you some of the news of what has passed before﴾, from the reports of the earlier nations, to multiply Your clear signs and to add to Your miracles. ﴿And We have indeed given you﴾, i.e., bestowed upon you, ﴿from Ourselves﴾, from Our presence, ﴿a reminder﴾, meaning the Qur'an. It is thus a great reminder and a noble Qur'an, in which there is salvation for whoever turns to it, and it comprises the narratives and reports that deserve reflection and lessons."

Whoever turns away from it (﴿مَن أعْرَضَ عَنْهُ﴾): from this Reminder, which is the Qur'an, and does not believe in it. (﴿فَإنَّهُ يَحْمِلُ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ وِزْرًا﴾) He will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden (wizr), a severe punishment. He called it a wizr as a metaphor for how heavy it is on the one being punished and how difficult it is to bear, likening it to a heavy load that breaks the back and leaves the one carrying it gasping (buhr). Or it is called that because it is the requital of the wizr, which is sin.

﴿Khālidīna﴾ (abiding eternally) is a ḥāl (circumstantial accusative) referring to the pronoun in yaḥmilu (he shall bear). It is pluralized according to the meaning, while the pronoun in fīhi (therein) is singular, in keeping with the wording of man (whoever). ﴿Fīhi﴾ (therein) refers to the burden, meaning in the recompense of the burden, which is the punishment. ﴿Wa-sāʾa lahum yawma al-qiyāmati ḥimlan﴾ (and evil is the burden for them on the Day of Resurrection). Sāʾa (it is evil) has the same ruling as biʾsa (how wretched), and within it is an undefined pronoun explained by ḥimlan, which is a tamyīz (specification). The lām in lahum is lil-bayān (for explanation), as in hayta laka (come, I am yours). The thing praised or blamed (al-makhṣūṣ bi-l-dhamm) is omitted, because the preceding word wizr (burden) indicates it. Its estimated form is: sāʾa al-ḥimlu ḥimlan wizruhum (evil is the burden, a burden being their load).

﴿On the day the Trumpet is blown﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "the Day of Resurrection." Abu 'Amr reads ﴿نَنْفُخُ﴾ (nanfukhu, "We blow"). ﴿In the Trumpet﴾: al-ṣūr is the horn, or it is the plural of ṣūra (form), meaning: We blow the spirits into the forms. The evidence for this is Qatada's recitation (qira'a), ﴿الصُوَرِ﴾ (al-ṣuwari), with a fatha on the waw, as the plural of ṣūra. ﴿And We shall gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed﴾: "blue-eyed" (zurqan) is a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning blind, as He said: ﴿And We shall gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind﴾ [al-Isra: 97]. This is because the pupil of the eye of one whose sight has gone turns blue (tazraqqu). (p-383)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 103:

﴿Yatakhafatūna﴾ (they will speak in low voices) yatasārrūna (they will speak secretly) ﴿baynahum﴾ (among themselves), i.e., some of them will say to others in secret, due to the terror of that Day. ﴿In labithtum﴾ (You remained not longer than) mā labithtum (you remained in the worldly life) ﴿illā ʿashran﴾ (except ten), i.e., ten nights.
