They will consider the duration of their stay to be short, whether in the graves or in the worldly life, because of the hardships they witness, which remind them of the days of blessing and joy, so they regret them and describe them as brief, because the days of joy are short. Or because those days have gone from them, and whatever has gone, however long its duration, is short by its ending. Or because of their sense that the Hereafter is long, since the lifespan of this world is always considered short in comparison to it, and the stay of its people in it is regarded as trifling when measured against their stay in the Hereafter. God has preferred the saying of the one who is most diminishing of them by His words: [the remainder of the commentary's quotation is cited in the text].

We know best what they say, when the most upright of them in conduct says, "You stayed only a day." (That is, the most just of them in speech.) And it is like His saying: "They will say: We stayed a day or part of a day; so ask those who count." (al-Mu'minun: 113)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 105:

﴿They ask you about the mountains.﴾ They asked the Prophet (ﷺ) what would be done with the mountains on the Day of Resurrection. It is also said that they did not ask; its implied sense is: "If they ask you," ﴿so say﴾. This is why the answer is joined with the fa' (the particle "fa", meaning "so"), unlike the other questions, such as His saying ﴿They ask you about menstruation. Say: It is a harm﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222], and His saying ﴿They ask you about orphans. Say: Setting things right for them is best﴾ [al-Baqarah: 220], ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling. Say: In both there is great sin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 219], ﴿They ask you about the Hour, when it will occur. Say: Its knowledge is only with my Lord﴾ [al-A'raf: 187], ﴿They ask you about the Spirit. Say: The Spirit is from the command of my Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 85], and ﴿They ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn. Say: I will recite to you some account of him﴾ [al-Kahf: 83]. These are questions that had already occurred, and their answers came, and they did not carry the meaning of a condition, so the fa' was not mentioned. ﴿My Lord will blow them away with a blast﴾, i.e., He will make them like sand, then send winds upon them which scatter them as grain is winnowed. Al-Khalil said: He will uproot them.

﴿So He will leave it﴾, meaning He will leave its places of settlement (*maqarr*). Or the pronoun may refer to the earth, though it is not mentioned, because it is known from context, as in His saying ﴿He leaves not a living creature upon its back﴾ [Fatir: 45]. ﴿A level plain, smooth﴾: even, flat, and free of any elevation or depression.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 107:

﴿You will not see in it any curvature﴾ meaning, depression, ﴿nor any elevation﴾ meaning, height. The word ʿiwaj (عِوَج) with a kasra on the ʿayn is used for what is abstract, just as the word with a fatha (عَوَج) is used for what is concrete. The earth is a concrete thing, but since the earth is leveled to such an evenness that no curvature can be found in it in any way, however subtle the device and however fine it may be, it takes on the status of abstract things.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 108:

﴿On that Day﴾ He attributed the day (al-yawm) to the time of the removal of the mountains, meaning: the day when they are removed. It is also permissible for it to be a second substitute (badal ba'd badal) for ﴿the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Ta-Ha: 101]. ﴿They will follow the summoner﴾ to the place of gathering (al-mahshar), meaning: the voice of the summoner, who is Israfil (Isrāfīl), when he calls out from the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem): "O decayed bones, torn skins, and scattered flesh, come forward to the presentation before the Most Merciful." So they come from every direction, heading toward his call, not turning away from it. ﴿There is no crookedness for him﴾ meaning: no one summoned deviates from it; rather they proceed straight toward it without swerving, following his voice. ﴿And the voices are humbled before the Most Merciful﴾ and become still, out of awe and reverence. ﴿So you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾: a faint sound produced by the moving of the lips. It is said that it derives from hamsu l-ibl (hams al-ibil), which is the sound of camels' feet when they walk, meaning: you will hear nothing but the fall of feet and their movement toward the place of gathering.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 109:

﴿On that Day, intercession will not benefit, except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, and whose word He has approved.﴾

The position of "man" (مَن) is nominative (raf'), as a substitute (badal) for "al-shafa'ah" (intercession), with the omission of a modifier (muḍāf) assumed; that is: intercession will not benefit except the intercession of one whom the Most Merciful has permitted, i.e., permission has been granted to the intercessor to intercede. ﴿And whose word He has approved﴾, i.e., Allah the Exalted is pleased with his word, on his account, by the condition that the one interceded for is a Muslim. Or it is in the accusative (naṣb) as the object (maf'ul) of "tanfa'" (will benefit).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 110:

﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾, i.e., He knows what has preceded them of circumstances and what they will face in the future. ﴿But they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾, i.e., they cannot encompass with knowledge that which God's knowledge encompasses. Thus the pronoun refers back to God, Exalted is He, because God, Exalted is He, is not encompassed by anything.

{And their faces will be humbled} — khadaʿat wa-dhallat (they were submissive and abased). From this comes the saying that a prisoner is ʿan (held captive). {The faces} — i.e., their owners, {before the Ever-Living} — who does not die; every life that is followed by death is as though it had never been, {the Self-Subsisting} — the Constantly Enduring, who stands over every soul for what it has earned; or, the one who stands in charge of the management of creation. {And he has failed} — yaʾisa min raḥmat Allah (he has despaired of the mercy of God), {he who carries wrongdoing} — he who carries shirk (association of partners with God) to the place of standing on the Day of Resurrection, because ẓulm (wrongdoing) is placing a thing in other than its proper place, and there is no greater wrongdoing than making a created being a partner to the One who created him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 112:

﴿And whoever does righteous deeds﴾ (al-salihat), meaning acts of obedience (al-ta'at), ﴿while he is a believer﴾ (mu'min), meaning one who affirms (musaddiq) what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought. In this is evidence that one deserves the name of faith (ism al-iman) without righteous deeds, and that faith is a condition for their acceptance (shart qabuliha). ﴿So he does not fear﴾, i.e., he does not fear, and "fa-la yakhaf" (so let him not fear) is read as a prohibition by Makki. ﴿Injustice (zulman)﴾, that an addition be made to his evil deeds, ﴿nor diminution (hadman)﴾, nor is anything reduced from his good deeds. The root meaning of hadm (diminution) is decrease (al-naqs) and breaking (al-kasr).

And similarly ﴿And thus﴾ is conjoined to "Thus We relate" (kadhalika naqussu), meaning: and like that revelation ﴿We revealed it as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ in the tongue of the Arabs, ﴿and We have varied﴾ (sarrafna), i.e., We repeated, ﴿within it some of the threat﴾ (al-wa'id), ﴿so that they may fear God﴾ (la'allahum yattaqun), i.e., that they may avoid shirk; ﴿or it may bring them﴾ (yuhdithu lahum), i.e., the threat or the Qur'an, ﴿a reminder﴾ (dhikran), i.e., an admonition, or honor through their faith in it. It is also said that "aw" here means "wa" (and).

﴿So exalted is Allah﴾ He is raised above the varieties of conjecture and the imaginings of minds, and He is transcendent above resemblance to created beings and likeness to bodies. ﴿The King﴾: the One whom kings need. ﴿The Truth﴾: the One who is true in His divinity (*ulūhiyya*). When He mentioned the Qur'an and its sending down, He said, by way of digression (*istitrād*): ﴿And when Jibril conveys to you what is revealed to you of the Qur'an, then take your time over it until he has made you hear and understood it.﴾ ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾ by reciting it ﴿before its revelation is completed for you﴾, that is, before Jibril has finished conveying it. ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ of the Qur'an and its meanings. It has also been said: Allah did not command His Messenger to seek increase in anything except knowledge. (p-386)

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 115:

﴿And We had certainly taken a covenant with Adam﴾, meaning: We revealed to him that he should not eat from the tree. In the orders and injunctions of kings it is said: "The king advanced toward so-and-so, instructed him (awʿaza ilayhi), resolved upon him (ʿazama ʿalayhi), and charged him (ʿahida ilayhi)." The story of Adam is thus joined (ʿuṭifat) to ﴿And We have diversified in it [the Qur'an] some of the threats﴾ [Ta-Ha: 113]. The meaning is: "I swear an oath that We had certainly commanded your father Adam and charged him not to approach the tree ﴿before﴾, that is, before their existence. Yet he deviated toward what he had been forbidden, just as they deviate." That is, the foundation of the command given to the children of Adam is upon this, and their disposition (ʿirq) is firmly rooted in it. ﴿But he forgot﴾, that is, the covenant, meaning the prohibition. The prophets, upon them be peace, are held accountable for forgetfulness which, had they exerted themselves, they would have guarded against. We did not find in him resolve (ʿazm), meaning a deliberate intent to oppose His command. Or Adam was not among the "possessors of resolve" (ulu al-ʿazm). The verb wajada may be used in the sense of knowing (ʿilm), in which case its two objects are: ʿazman (resolve) and the phrase introduced by lahu (for him). Or it may be used in the sense of the opposite of non-existence (ʿadam), meaning: "We did not make resolve exist in him." The phrase lahu (for him) is attached to najid (we found).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 116:

﴿And when We said to the angels: "Prostrate to Adam"﴾ is governed by (manṣūb bi) "udhkur" (remember). ﴿To the angels: "Prostrate to Adam."﴾ It has been said that this is the linguistic prostration (al-sujūd al-lughawī), which is submission (al-khuḍūʿ) and humbling oneself (al-tadhallul); or Adam was like a qibla, a means of showing reverence to him. ﴿So they prostrated, except Iblis.﴾ On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, Iblis was an angel of the kind of those excepted from them. Al-Ḥasan said: The angels are the essence (lubāb) of creation from among the spirits, and they do not reproduce, while Iblis is from the fire of the simoom (nār al-samūm). The exception from them is valid only because he used to accompany them and worship Allah with them. ﴿He refused (abā)⦆ is a resumed sentence (jumla mustaʾnafa), as if it were an answer to someone who asked: "Why did he not prostrate?" The preferable view is that no object be assumed for it, namely the prostration indicated by His saying "so they prostrated," and that its meaning be: he showed refusal (al-ibāʾ) and hesitated.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 117:

﴿Then We said, "O Adam, indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife."﴾ [when he did not prostrate and did not see your superiority] ﴿So let him not expel you both from the Garden, [and thus you suffer]﴾ meaning, let him not become a cause of your expulsion ﴿and you will be distressed﴾ meaning, you will exert yourself in seeking sustenance. And it was not said "fa-tashqa" (both of you will be distressed) out of consideration for the rhyme-endings of the verses (ru'us al-ayy), or because it follows the masculine form (dakhalat tab'an); or because the man is the one responsible for the maintenance of the woman. It is narrated that a red bull was sent down to Adam, and he would plough with it and wipe the sweat from his brow.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 118:

﴿Indeed, for you there is that you will not hunger therein﴾ in the Garden, ﴿and you will not be naked﴾ of garments, because they (the garments) are prepared therein forever.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 119:

﴿And that you﴾ with kasra is read by Nafi' and Abu Bakr, as a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the first inna (إنَّ الأُولى). The rest read it with fatha, as a conjunction upon ﴿that you will not hunger﴾ [Ta-Ha: 118]. Its place (mahall) is in the accusative by inna, and it is permissible because of the intervening element (li-l-fasl), as you say: "Indeed, in my knowledge that you are sitting." ﴿You will not thirst therein﴾, i.e., you will not be parched, because of the existence of drinks therein. ﴿Nor will you be exposed to the sun﴾, i.e., the heat of the sun will not strike you, since there is no sun there; its people are in extended shade.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 120:

﴿Then Satan whispered to him.﴾ That is: he conveyed the whisper to him, as one says "asarra ilayhi" (he confided to him in secret). ﴿He said: "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity and a kingdom that does not decay?"﴾ He attributed the tree to eternity (al-khuld), which is immortality, because whoever eats from it, by his claim, will live forever and not die. ﴿And a kingdom that does not decay﴾: that does not perish.

﴿فَأكَلا﴾, meaning Adam and Hawwa', ﴿مِنها فَبَدَتْ لَهُما سَوْآتُهُما﴾: "they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them." ﴿وَطَفِقا﴾: *ṭafiqa* (طَفِقَ) means "he began to do such-and-such," like *jaʿala* (جَعَلَ) "he began to do." It is like *kāda* (كادَ) in that the predicate is a present-tense verb, except that *ṭafiqa* indicates the beginning of an action at its outset, while *kāda* indicates approaching it. ﴿يَخْصِفانِ عَلَيْهِما مِن ورَقِ الجَنَّةِ﴾, meaning they began to stick leaves onto their private parts to cover them, and these were fig leaves. ﴿وَعَصى آدَمُ رَبَّهُ فَغَوى﴾: *faghawā* means he strayed from the right opinion (*ḍalla ʿan al-raʾy*). According to Ibn ʿĪsā, it means he failed (*khāba*). The summary is that *ʿiṣyān* (disobedience) is the doing of an act contrary to a command or prohibition. It may be deliberate, in which case it is a sin (*dhanb*), or it may not be deliberate, in which case it is a slip (*zallah*). Since his act was described as disobedience, it was removed from being right guidance, so it was misguidance (*ghayy*), because *ghayy* is the opposite of *rushd* (right guidance). In stating ﴿وَعَصى آدَمُ رَبَّهُ فَغَوى﴾ explicitly, and in turning away from saying "Adam slipped" (*wa-zalla Ādam*), there is a powerful deterrent and an admonition addressed to all the responsible (*mukallafīn*), as if it were said to them: look, or take heed, at how his slip was condemned with this severity, the infallible Prophet, the beloved of God. So do not be lax about the minor faults (*ṣaghāʾir*) that come from you, let alone the major ones (*kabāʾir*).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 122:

﴿Then his Lord chose him﴾ He drew him near to Himself and chose him for Himself, and it is also read with this meaning. The root of the word is gathering; it is said: "Such-and-such was gathered (judiya) to me," so I gathered it (ijtabaytuhu). ﴿So He accepted his repentance﴾ He received his repentance. ﴿And guided him﴾ He guided him to seeking excuse and asking for forgiveness.

"He said: Go down from it, all of you" — meaning Adam and Eve — "some of you" — O children of Adam — "to others an enemy" through envy in the world and difference in religion. "But if there comes to you from Me guidance" — a Book and a law — "then whoever follows My guidance will not go astray" in this world, "nor will he be distressed" in the Hereafter.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: Allah guaranteed to whoever follows the Qur'an that he will not go astray in this world and will not be distressed in the Hereafter. That is to say: the distress in the Hereafter is the punishment of the one who strayed in this world from the path of religion. Whoever follows the Book of Allah, carries out its commands, and refrains from its prohibitions, is saved from straying and from its punishment.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 124:

﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance﴾ — from the Qur'an — ﴿indeed, for him is a constricted life﴾ — narrowness. It is a verbal noun (maṣdar) which is used as a description for both the masculine and the feminine. From Ibn Jubayr: "It deprives him of contentment, so that he is never satisfied. With religion there is submission, contentment and reliance upon God, so his life is good; but with turning away there is greed and avarice, so his living is constricted and his state is dark." As some of the Sufis said: "None of you turns away from the remembrance of his Lord without his time being darkened for him and his provision being disturbed for him." ﴿And We will raise him on the Day of Resurrection blind﴾ — from the proof. From Ibn 'Abbas: blind of sight. This is like His saying: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces, blind, mute and deaf﴾ [al-Isra: 97], and this is the face.
﴿He will say, "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, when I was seeing?"﴾ in the world.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 126:

﴿He said: "Thus"﴾ — i.e., "In the same way did you act." Then he explained it, saying: ﴿"Our signs came to you, but you forgot them; and thus today you are forgotten."﴾ — i.e., Our signs came to you clear and plain, but you did not look upon them with the eye of one who takes heed, you abandoned them, and you became blind to them. So, in the same way, today We leave you in your blindness and do not remove its covering from your eyes.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 127:

﴿And thus do We recompense those who transgress and do not believe in the signs of their Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more enduring.﴾ When He threatened the one who turns away from His remembrance with two punishments, a constricted life in this world and being raised blind on the Day of Reckoning, He concluded the verses of warning with His words, ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more enduring.﴾ That is: the being gathered blind, which never ends, is more severe than the narrow hardship of life, which comes to an end.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 128:

﴿Afa-lam yahdi lahum﴾ — i.e., Allah — according to the reading of Zayd on the authority of Ya'qub, with the nun (﴿Afa-lam nahdi lahum﴾, "Will We not guide them?"). ﴿How many generations We destroyed before them, while they walk in their dwellings﴾ — the phrase ﴿yamshuna﴾ ("they walk") is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in ﴿lahum﴾. ﴿In their dwellings﴾ — he means that the Quraysh walk through the dwellings of ʿAd, Thamud and the people of Lut, and witness the traces of their destruction. ﴿Surely in that are signs for people of understanding﴾ — for those with intellects; when they reflect, they know that their annihilation was because of their disbelief, so they do not do the like of what they did.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 129:

﴿Had it not been for a word that had already gone forth from your Lord﴾, i.e., the decree to postpone the punishment from the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), ﴿it would have been inevitable﴾, i.e., binding. Al-lizam (inevitability) is a verbal noun from lazima (to be bound to, to be necessary), and it is used as a description (of the punishment). ﴿And a term appointed﴾, namely the Resurrection, is conjoined to ﴿a word﴾. The meaning is: Had it not been for a decree that had gone forth to postpone the punishment from them, and an appointed term, which is the Resurrection, the punishment would have been inevitably binding upon them in this world, just as it was binding upon the earlier disbelieving generations.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 130:

﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ concerning you, ﴿and glorify﴾ and pray ﴿with the praise of your Lord﴾. This is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: while you are praising your Lord for having enabled you to glorify Him and having helped you to do so (p-390) ﴿before the rising of the sun﴾, meaning: the dawn prayer (ṣalāt al-fajr); ﴿and before its setting﴾, meaning: the noon prayer (al-ẓuhr) and the afternoon prayer (al-ʿaṣr), because both fall in the last half of the day, between the decline of the sun and its setting. ﴿And during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day﴾, meaning: and devote yourself to the hours of the night, that is, its periods, "and the ends of the day", specifically dedicating these to your prayer. Glorification during the hours of the night includes the ʿatamah prayer (ṣalāt al-ʿatamah, the night prayer), and at the ends of the day it includes the maghrib prayer (ṣalāt al-maghrib) and the fajr prayer, by repetition, intending particularity, just as the "middle prayer" (al-ṣalāh al-wusṭā) is singled out in His saying according to some scholars. The plural "ends" (aṭrāf) is used for the two ends (ṭarafān) because there is no risk of confusion. ﴿So that you may be pleased﴾ is coordinated with "before" (qabla). The "la'alla" here addresses the Prophet: remember God at these times, hoping that you will attain with God what will satisfy your soul and gladden your heart. "Turḍā" is read by ʿAlī and Abū Bakr, meaning: your Lord will please you.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 131:**

﴿And do not extend your eyes﴾: that is, the gaze of your eyes. Extending the gaze (*madd al-nazar*) means prolonging it so that one almost never turns it back, out of admiration for the thing looked at and being impressed by it. In this is the indication that a gaze that is not prolonged is pardoned, namely when one glances at a thing and then lowers the gaze. The pious have been strict about the obligation to lower the gaze from the buildings of the oppressors and the number of the wicked in their clothing and mounts, to the extent that al-Hasan said: "Do not look at the jingling of the wicked's well-fed (*hamalij*) [mounts]; rather, look at how the humiliation of sin shows on those necks!" This is because they only adopted these things for the eyes of onlookers, so whoever looks at them accomplishes their aim and tempts them to adopt them.

﴿to that which We have given enjoyment to, pairs of them﴾: that is, kinds of disbelievers. It is permissible that *azwajan* (pairs) be parsed as a circumstantial accusative (*hal*) from the *ha'* of the pronoun, with the verb falling on *minhum* (of them), as if he said: "to that which We gave enjoyment to, which is kinds, some of them and some people among them."

﴿the splendor of the worldly life﴾: its adornment and its brilliance. It is in the accusative either as a dispraise (*dhamm*), or as a substitution (*ibdal*) from the position of *bihi* (with it), or as a substitution from *azwajan* (pairs), on the estimate of "those possessing the splendor."

﴿so that We may test them therein﴾: that We may try them, so that they deserve the punishment because of the disbelief present in them, or that We may punish them in the Hereafter because of it.

﴿But the provision of your Lord﴾: its reward, which is Paradise, or the lawful sufficiency. ﴿is better and more enduring﴾ than what they have been provided with.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 132:

﴿And enjoin your family﴾ (your community, ummah, or the people of your household) ﴿to prayer, and persevere in it﴾ (you, persist in it). ﴿We do not ask you for provision﴾ (i.e., We do not ask you to provide sustenance for yourself or for your family). ﴿We provide for you﴾ and for them, so do not concern yourself with the matter of provision, and free your mind for the matter of the Hereafter, for whoever is occupied with the work of Allah, Allah will be occupied with his affairs. It is narrated from ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr that when he saw what was in the possession of rulers (al-salatin), he would recite ﴿And do not extend your eyes [toward what We have given to some pairs of them]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 131], the verse, then call out, "Prayer, prayer, may Allah have mercy on you." Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani, whenever his family suffered hardship (khasasah), would say, "Stand up and pray." It was with this that Allah commanded His Messenger. It is also narrated from Malik ibn Dinar something similar. And in some of the musnad collections: "Indeed, when the Prophet (ﷺ) saw that his family was in distress, he would command them to pray and recite this verse."

﴿And the good outcome is for the righteous (taqwa)﴾: that is, the good outcome belongs to the people of taqwa (God-consciousness), with two elements omitted (i.e., the word for "people" and the word for "those who fear," so the sense is: the good end is for the people of taqwa).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 133:

﴿And they say﴾, i.e., the disbelievers, ﴿"Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?"﴾ Meaning: "Why does Muhammad not bring us a sign from his Lord that shows the soundness of his prophethood?" ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ The reading here is that of Madani, Basri and Hafs. ﴿The former scriptures﴾, i.e., the earlier books. The meaning is: they proposed, out of their habit of obstinacy, a sign for prophethood, so it was said to them: "Has there not come to you a sign that is the mother of signs and the greatest of them in the matter of inimitability, namely the Qur'an? For the Qur'an is a proof of what is in all the revealed books and evidence of their soundness, because it is a miracle, whereas those (earlier books) are not miracles; they therefore depend on its testimony for the soundness of what is in them."

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 20, verse 134:

﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it [i.e., before the Messenger and the Qur'an]﴾, [they would have said], ﴿"Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger, so that we might follow Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced"﴾. [In the Arabic, the word] ﴿لَوْلا﴾ [means] ﴿هَلّا﴾ (why not). [The verb] ﴿فَنَتَّبِعَ﴾ (so that we might follow) is in the subjunctive (naṣb) because it is the answer (jawāb) to the interrogative (istifhām) by means of the fā' [of result]. ﴿أنْ نَذِلَّ﴾ (that we be humiliated) [means] by the descent of punishment, ﴿وَنَخْزى﴾ (and be disgraced) [means] in the Hereafter.

**Al-Nasafi, *Madarik al-Tanzil*, on Surah 20, verse 135:**

﴿Say: "Each [of us]"﴾, that is, each one of us and of you, ﴿is waiting﴾, awaiting the outcome and what our affair and yours will lead to. ﴿So wait﴾, you, ﴿and you will soon know﴾ when the Resurrection comes ﴿who are the companions of﴾ the ﴿even path﴾, the straight one, ﴿and who has been guided﴾ to the enduring bliss.

Here, ﴿مَن أصْحابُ﴾ (man aṣḥābu, "who are the companions of") is a *mubtada'* (مُبْتَدَأٌ, subject of a nominal sentence) and *khabar* (خَبَرٌ, predicate), and their grammatical position (*maḥall*) is accusative (*naṣb*).

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The people of Paradise will recite only *Ṭāhā* and *Yā-Sīn*."

And Allah knows best what is correct.
